strengths: The paper addresses a consequential evaluation problem for brain-to-text NLP: distinguishing generalization to new subjects and new linguistic stimuli from performance benefiting from overlap with training data.
Separating subject overlap, stimulus overlap, and overlapping fMRI windows is useful. Requiring disjoint subjects and stimuli is a sensible criterion for the stated joint generalization target.

Experiments cover two modalities, two established models, and several splitting strategies, with additional-test-set and shuffled-input controls. Table 6 also reports evaluation without teacher forcing and retains differences between splitting strategies, providing some support for the underlying concern.
weaknesses: The central benchmark still uses teacher forcing during evaluation. Table 6 identifies the scores reused in Tables 3–5 as teacher-forced results. Providing gold prefixes changes the task and confounds the interpretation of shuffled-input robustness as memorization caused by training-set overlap. Table 6 is a useful partial correction, but the additional-test-set and shuffled-input comparisons are not repeated without teacher forcing. Autonomous generation should be the primary benchmark.

The published algorithms do not implement the claimed disjointness guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, restricts the subject when expanding training data but permits stimuli assigned to validation or test. Algorithm 2, line 33, restricts the story but permits held-out subjects. These steps can reintroduce the overlaps prohibited by the mathematical criterion. Corrected pseudocode and verification of the actual experimental partitions are necessary.

Several causal interpretations are unsupported. Decreasing validation reconstruction loss in Figure 5 does not demonstrate that encoder representations are deteriorating. Continuing improvement with longer training also does not establish leakage. Moreover, changing splits changes subject/story distributions and, through discarding data, potentially training-set size. Controlled comparisons on common held-out data with matched training budgets are needed to attribute performance differences specifically to overlap.

The formal leakage metrics are inconsistent with their intended meaning. Equation 17 counts intersecting signal instances rather than shared subject identities: distinct EEG samples from the same subject can occupy separate partitions without any signal-instance intersection, yet Table 2 reports positive BSLR. Equations 6–7 also quantify over every training example, although even partial overlap can violate the criterion. The definitions and reported computations need reconciliation.

Numerical reporting requires an audit. Table 5 gives EEG2Text ROUGE precision 23.95, recall 23.98, and F-score 25.74, which is incompatible with standard consistent aggregation. Several values labeled ROUGE recall in Table 7 appear as ROUGE F-score in Table 3. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the benchmark values and model comparisons.

The universal claims exceed the evidence. Joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli is a specific evaluation target. Testing unseen subjects on familiar stimuli can address a different legitimate question, although it cannot establish novel-stimulus generalization. The assertions that all current splitting methods are wrong and their evaluations meaningless should be narrowed to the claims and protocols actually examined.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for a benchmark contribution. Despite useful hyperparameters in Appendix B, the manuscript does not provide exact retained split counts and identities, discarded-data fractions, a reproducible construction of the additional test set, precise shuffling details, or a code/split-artifact link. Only leakage statistics receive repeated-seed uncertainty estimates. These gaps and the evaluation and algorithmic problems prevent a sound Findings recommendation; corrected experiments and documentation could support resubmission next cycle.

strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem in brain-to-text decoding: subject overlap and repeated text stimuli can undermine claims of generalization. Explicitly separating these dependencies, including overlapping fMRI windows, is useful.

The empirical audit covers two modalities, two established models, and several splitting strategies. Additional held-out data and shuffled-input controls provide informative diagnostics of apparent decoding performance.

Appendix Table 6 shows that performance differences between splits persist under decoding without teacher forcing, supporting a narrower concern about split sensitivity. Public datasets and reported hyperparameters provide a useful starting point for replication.
weaknesses: The main results, including the 'fair benchmark' in Table 5, use teacher-forced evaluation, as Table 6 confirms. Providing gold prefixes substantially changes the task and confounds the interpretation of resilience to shuffled brain inputs. Although Table 6 supplies free-generation results, the additional-test-set and shuffled-input controls are not repeated under that setting. Consequently, the central attribution to split leakage and the proposed generation benchmark remain inadequately validated.

The pseudocode does not enforce the claimed exclusion rules as written. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership but can add training edges containing validation/test text. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks story membership but can add validation/test subjects to training. These conditions contradict the joint restrictions in the main formulation. Corrected executable splitting code and explicit overlap audits are needed to establish that the experimental splits actually satisfy the proposed criterion.

Formal definitions and reported metrics contain consequential inconsistencies. Definitions 3.1–3.2 require overlap for every training example, although partial overlap already constitutes leakage. Equation 17 measures shared signal instances despite defining leakage through shared subjects. ROUGE values also conflict: Tables 3–4 label 40.65 as F-score where Table 7 labels it recall; Table 5 reports EEG2Text F=25.74 with P=23.95 and R=23.98, inconsistent with standard aggregation. These issues weaken confidence in the quantitative audit.

Essential replication and comparison details are missing: actual subject/story assignments, retained and discarded sample counts, and the size and construction of the additional test set. No code or split-manifest link is provided. A nominal 80/10/10 ratio does not control training volume or test difficulty when different methods discard different data. Four seeds are reported for leakage rates, but uncertainty across model runs and subject/story splits is not reported.

The encoder-overfitting interpretation is not established. Decreasing reconstruction validation loss on familiar subjects does not demonstrate deteriorating representations on unseen subjects; an independent transfer evaluation is required. Similarly, improving test scores with longer training does not itself diagnose leakage. The supplementary comparison also changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together, preventing a clean causal interpretation.

The claim that all existing splitting methods are wrong exceeds the evidence and conflates distinct evaluation targets. New-subject decoding of familiar stimuli and new-stimulus decoding for familiar subjects can be legitimate protocols when their scope is explicit. The proposed criterion targets joint generalization to unseen subjects and stimuli. The contribution is relevant, but the evaluation, split-correctness, and reporting issues prevent a Findings recommendation; focused corrections and experimental reruns could support resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text NLP: shared subjects, repeated linguistic stimuli, and overlapping fMRI windows can undermine claims of generalization. An evaluation audit is a worthwhile contribution without requiring a new decoding architecture.

Experiments cover two established models and both EEG and fMRI. The substantial performance gaps on additional held-out data and the persistence of high scores after input shuffling provide concerning evidence about existing evaluation practices. Table 6 usefully shows that differences between splitting methods persist without teacher forcing.

Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli is a sensible protocol for evaluating generalization to new people and new linguistic content. The graph illustrations communicate these dependencies, and the paper acknowledges the cost of discarding samples.
weaknesses: The main evaluation remains confounded by teacher forcing. Table 6 establishes that the headline results, including the 'fair benchmark' in Table 5, use gold previous tokens during decoding. These measure prediction with privileged linguistic context rather than autonomous brain-to-text generation. The non-teacher-forced results are a useful partial check, but the additional-test and shuffled-input controls are not repeated under that setting. Those controls and the principal benchmark should use generation without gold prefixes.

The published algorithms do not implement the claimed zero-leakage guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, excludes held-out subjects but does not exclude held-out texts when expanding training data. Algorithm 2, line 33, excludes held-out stories but does not exclude held-out subjects. These steps can reintroduce exactly the overlaps prohibited by the mathematical constraints. This could be a pseudocode error, but corrected executable code and audits of the actual experimental splits are necessary to establish which procedure produced the results.

Several formal definitions are incorrect as written. Equations 6–7 require every training example to have a matching subject or stimulus in the test set, whereas even partial overlap should satisfy the intended leakage definition. Equation 17 intersects signal identities, although subject overlap can occur with entirely distinct recordings; it also lacks a convention for a zero denominator when a test subject is absent from training. Consequently, the reported BSLR values cannot be reliably reconstructed from the stated definition.

The experiments do not adequately isolate leakage from other consequences of changing splits. Holding out subjects and stimuli changes distribution, difficulty, and available training data simultaneously. The paper gives an 80:10:10 ratio but no resulting sample counts, discarded-data proportions, or sufficiently precise construction of the additional test set. A documented common clean evaluation set and training-size controls would strengthen the causal interpretation. Decoding results also lack uncertainty across training seeds or subject/stimulus partitions; the four-seed analysis covers only leakage metrics.

The claims about encoder overfitting are not demonstrated by Figure 5. Decreasing validation reconstruction loss does not establish that representations are degrading, and continued improvement in test scores is not itself proof of leakage or overfitting. These claims require learning curves on an independent, appropriately held-out population or another direct generalization measure. The EEG curves do not corroborate the proposed distinction between encoders trained with and without subject overlap.

Reproducibility and reporting need correction. Appendix B supplies some hyperparameters, but no code or fixed split-manifest release is identified, and the precise shuffling operation is unspecified. There are also substantive metric inconsistencies: Table 5 reports EEG2Text ROUGE-F of 25.74 despite precision and recall of 23.95 and 23.98, which is incompatible with conventional F1 aggregation. Tables 3 and 7 label the same Narratives value, 40.65, as F and recall respectively.

The universal framing exceeds the supported contribution. Subject-only and stimulus-only splits can answer legitimate, narrower generalization questions; they are not automatically invalid because they fail the proposed joint-generalization criterion. The paper should map criticized practices to the original studies' claimed targets and qualify statements that all existing evaluations are 'meaningless.' The evaluation, algorithmic, and reproducibility concerns above prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current version, but appear addressable in a next-cycle revision.
